newsitem.title: USA: U.N. arms sleuth in Iraq plans new approach.
newsitem.headline: U.N. arms sleuth in Iraq plans new approach.

text.p: The U.N. official in charge of destroying Iraq's deadliest weapons said on Tuesday he would try a new tack with Iraqi political leaders next month in an effort to win their cooperation.

Rolf Ekeus, the Swedish diplomat who heads the special U.N. arms-disposal commission, said he would confront Deputy Prime Minister Tariq Aziz with what U.N. inspectors know about missing Iraqi ballistic missiles rather than wait for an Iraqi accounting.
"We will turn it upside down," he said of the routine approach, which requires Iraq to declare banned weapons and other material Iraq promised to destroy after being defeated in the 1991 Gulf War.

Ekeus described the fresh approach as a possible one-shot deal that could set the stage for Iraqi political leaders to "come clean" on banned nuclear, chemical and biological weapons, a prerequisite for the U.N. Security Council to consider lifting economic sanctions.

He said he would meet Tariq Aziz in Baghdad in the "first part" of next month to pose the missing missile issue on a political rather than a technical level. Ekeus said as many as 16 missiles were unaccounted for. He said finding out what happened to them could lead to quick progress on other issues, such as chemical and biological arms that could be delivered in warheads.
He said Tariq Aziz recently visited Moscow in an apparent effort to prepare for the session with information about missiles supplied by Moscow to Baghdad before the Gulf War.

"It can be an important meeting," Ekeus said, calling it a chance for the political leadership "to start to solve the problem ... to get the embargo lifted." Ekeus made his remarks to a forum organised by the Centre for Strategic and International Studies, a private foreign policy research organisation.

He said his U.N. Special Commission on Iraq, which runs no-notice, highly intrusive inspections by about 100 U.N. personnel based in Baghdad, was running out of funds to operate. The commission had been scheduled to collect much of its $36 million in annual operating expenses from the suspended plan to let Iraq sell up to $2 billion in oil for relief supplies over a six-month period, a plan held up after Iraqi troops pushed into Kurdish territority in August, setting off U.S. missile retaliation.

Ekeus said the new effort to pitch the political leadership followed a determination that the Iraqi Republican Guard and intelligence agencies had been involved in a "systematic" effort to conceal banned weapons and Iraqi capabilities. But he said the decision to go on hiding weapons appeared to be a political decision designed to hang on to power to influence events outside Iraq's borders.

Among the weapons apparently still being hidden, he said, were biological agents such as Anthrax that could potentially be used in warheads to threaten cities throughout the Middle East if Iraq were allowed to develop the capability to deliver them reliably.
"When we talk about threats in the Middle East, this is probably number one," said Judith Kipper, co-director of the CSIS Middle Eastern programme.

Anthony Cordesman, a former Pentagon strategist who is the program's other co-director, said that without supervision Iraq retained the capabilty to produce covertly significant amounts of easily delivered dry Anthrax aerosols in six to 12 months. He said Iraq would not need missiles to use them.

If a dozen immunised terrorists took attache cases with a total of 100 kilograms (220 pounds) of anthrax to the top of tall buildings in places such as Ankara, Riyadh, Jerusalem, Cairo, Tehran, Isfahan or Damascus they could kill as many as 3 million people under certain weather conditions, he said.
